course.title: Startup Fundraising & Venture Capital
course.description: Startup fundraising explained for founders and operators - how companies raise money, from bootstrapping and the funding stages to valuation, cap tables, term sheets, and alternatives like crowdfunding and grants. It covers who invests, how venture capital actually works, and the instruments and process behind a modern raise, kept practical and balanced. Structure adapted from the Venture capital article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

lessons.title: Bootstrapping vs. raising outside money
lessons.grammar_note: When you say you 'raised' money, remember you also 'sold' a share of the company - both are true at once.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Decide, for a given startup, whether to bootstrap or raise outside money, and explain the trade-offs in ownership, speed, and control. Warm-up: if you fund your company only from its own sales and your savings, who owns it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Bootstrapping means building a company using personal savings, early revenue, and hard work rather than outside investment. You keep full ownership and answer to no one, but growth is capped by the cash the business itself produces. Raising money means selling a slice of the company to investors in exchange for cash you can spend now. That cash can buy speed - hiring ahead of revenue, building before customers arrive, and outrunning rivals - but it comes with new owners who expect a large return and a say in big decisions. Neither path is better in itself. Bootstrapping suits businesses with low startup costs, quick revenue, and founders who value control. Raising suits businesses that need heavy upfront spending, that win by growing faster than competitors, or that chase a market so large investors will pay for a shot at it. Many companies that raise still bootstrap first, using early traction to prove the idea before trading equity for fuel.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example 1: a consulting firm bills clients from month one, so it can bootstrap and may never need investors. Example 2: a hardware company must build a production line before a single unit ships, so it almost certainly raises. Example 3: founders bootstrap to a working product and ten paying customers, then raise a seed round at a far higher valuation than they could have gotten on day one, giving away less ownership for the same cash. The core trade-off is ownership versus speed. Suppose a founder owns 100 percent of a company worth 1 million dollars. If she raises 500,000 dollars at a 2 million dollar pre-money valuation, the company is now worth 2.5 million, she owns 80 percent, and her stake is worth 2 million dollars - more than before, on a bigger pie. Raising is not free money; it is a sale of future upside, justified only when the cash makes the whole pie grow faster than the slice you give away.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A company funds growth only from its profits. What is this called? 2) True or false: raising money always makes the founder poorer. 3) Name one business type that is a natural fit for bootstrapping. 4) If you raise 250,000 dollars at a 1 million dollar pre-money valuation, what percentage do investors own? 5) Why might founders bootstrap first and raise later? Answers: 1) bootstrapping. 2) False - a smaller slice of a much larger company can be worth more. 3) a service or consulting business with fast revenue and low costs. 4) post-money is 1.25 million, so 250,000 / 1,250,000 = 20 percent. 5) early traction raises the valuation, so they give away less ownership for the same cash.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating raised money as a prize rather than a sale of ownership you must justify with faster growth. Mistake: bootstrapping a business that structurally needs heavy upfront capital, then stalling for lack of cash. Exit ticket: (a) In one sentence, what does bootstrapping mean? (b) Raising money trades what for what? Answers: (a) funding the company from savings and its own revenue instead of outside investors; (b) it trades a share of future ownership for cash you can spend now to grow faster.

lessons.title: The funding stages: pre-seed to growth
lessons.grammar_note: Round names (pre-seed, seed, Series A) are labels for a stage, not legal categories - use them loosely.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the common startup funding stages in order and describe what a company is expected to have achieved at each one. Warm-up: which usually comes first, a seed round or a Series A?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Startup funding tends to arrive in named rounds, each matching a stage of maturity. Pre-seed is the earliest: a small amount, often from founders, friends, or angels, to turn an idea into a prototype. Seed money funds the search for product-market fit - building the first real product and finding early customers. Series A is the first large institutional round, raised once a company shows a repeatable way to acquire customers and real revenue; the money scales what already works. Series B expands a proven business with more hires and more markets. Series C and later rounds fund large-scale growth, acquisitions, or the run-up to going public. Growth rounds are large, later-stage investments in companies that are already sizable and often nearing profitability. The labels are conventions, not rules; a company can skip a letter or raise two seed rounds. Each later stage usually means a higher valuation, more money raised, and more scrutiny, because investors are buying into less risk and more evidence.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Rough, non-binding patterns help set expectations. Pre-seed might be tens to a few hundred thousand dollars for a prototype. Seed might be one to three million dollars to reach product-market fit. A Series A might be five to twenty million dollars once revenue is growing predictably. Series B and C grow from there, often into the tens or hundreds of millions. Example: a team raises 150,000 dollars pre-seed to build a demo, then a 2 million dollar seed round to ship the product and sign the first fifty customers. With revenue climbing a steady 15 percent each month, they raise a 12 million dollar Series A to hire a sales team and expand. Each round answers a different question: pre-seed asks 'can we build it?', seed asks 'do people want it?', and Series A asks 'can we grow it profitably and fast?' Matching your round to the question you can honestly answer is how you raise at a fair valuation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Put these in order: Series A, seed, pre-seed. 2) At which stage is a company mainly searching for product-market fit? 3) What question does a Series A round typically answer? 4) True or false: a company must raise every round in the alphabet. 5) Why do later rounds usually come at higher valuations? Answers: 1) pre-seed, seed, Series A. 2) seed. 3) can we grow revenue profitably and fast? 4) false - the labels are conventions and companies skip or repeat rounds. 5) later rounds carry less risk and more evidence, so investors pay more per share.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: raising a large Series A before you can show a repeatable way to win customers - the money then funds guesswork, not scaling. Mistake: treating the dollar ranges as hard rules; they vary widely by sector and region. Exit ticket: (a) Which round is the first large institutional round? (b) What is a growth round? Answers: (a) Series A; (b) a large, later-stage investment in a company that is already sizable and often close to profitability.

lessons.title: Who invests, and how venture capital works
lessons.grammar_note: Keep 'the fund' (the pool of money) separate from 'the firm' (the people who manage it) when you read venture news.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify the main sources of startup capital and explain how a venture capital fund actually makes money. Warm-up: when a venture firm invests, whose money is it usually spending?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Early money comes from several sources. Friends and family invest small amounts out of trust, early and informally. Angel investors are wealthy individuals who put their own money into young companies, often adding advice and introductions. Accelerators give a small sum, mentorship, and a demo day in exchange for a slice of equity over a fixed program. Venture capital firms invest larger, pooled money in companies aiming to grow very fast. A venture fund does not spend the partners' own savings; it raises a pool from limited partners - pension funds, university endowments, and wealthy families - who want exposure to high-growth startups. The firm's general partners choose the investments, sit on boards, and help companies grow. They are paid a yearly management fee, often about 2 percent of the fund, plus carried interest, usually about 20 percent of the profits. So a fund only truly succeeds for its partners when the companies it backs become far more valuable.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: The returns of a venture fund follow a power law: a few investments return almost everything, and most return little or nothing. Suppose a fund makes twenty investments. Perhaps half fail completely, a handful return the money, and one becomes a huge success that pays for the entire fund several times over. Because of this, venture capitalists chase companies with the potential to grow 10 or 100 times, not safe bets that might double. A company that could grow steadily but modestly is a poor fit for venture money, even if it is a fine business. Example: a 100 million dollar fund needs to return several hundred million to satisfy its limited partners. One investment that turns 2 million dollars into 300 million can carry the whole fund, which is exactly why a venture investor would rather fund ten risky long shots than one safe, small win. Understanding this math explains why venture capitalists push for aggressive growth.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who provides the money that a venture fund invests? 2) Name two sources of early startup capital besides venture capital. 3) What are the two main ways a venture firm gets paid? 4) In one sentence, what is the power law of venture returns? 5) Why is a steady, modestly growing business a poor fit for venture money? Answers: 1) limited partners, such as pension funds and endowments. 2) any two of: friends and family, angel investors, accelerators. 3) a management fee (around 2 percent per year) and carried interest (around 20 percent of profits). 4) a few investments produce almost all of the returns while most produce little. 5) venture math needs a few giant outcomes, so a capped upside cannot pay for the many losses.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming venture capitalists invest their own money - they mostly invest their limited partners' money and answer to them. Mistake: pitching a solid but slow-growing business to venture firms, whose model requires a chance at enormous outcomes. Exit ticket: (a) What is carried interest? (b) What does the power law imply about how venture capitalists pick companies? Answers: (a) the share of a fund's profits, usually about 20 percent, that the general partners keep; (b) they favor companies with a real chance of growing enormously, since a few winners must pay for many losses.

lessons.title: Valuation, equity, dilution, and cap tables
lessons.grammar_note: Watch the difference between shares (a count) and percentage (a share of the whole) - dilution changes the percentage, not your share count.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a simple cap table, compute how a funding round dilutes existing owners, and tell pre-money from post-money valuation. Warm-up: if a company is worth 4 million dollars before an investment and raises 1 million, what is it worth right after?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Equity is ownership, usually measured in shares. A cap table (capitalization table) is the list of who owns how many shares and what percentage each stake represents. When a company raises money, it issues new shares and sells them to investors. Pre-money valuation is what the company is judged to be worth just before the new money arrives; post-money valuation is pre-money plus the amount raised. The investor's ownership equals the amount they put in divided by the post-money valuation. Issuing new shares means every existing owner now holds a smaller percentage of the company - this is dilution. Dilution is not automatically bad: your slice shrinks, but if the round makes the whole company more valuable, your slice can still be worth more in dollars. Founders also set aside an option pool, a block of shares reserved for future employees, which dilutes the founders too. Reading a cap table is simply tracking these percentages as rounds and pools stack up.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example: a founder owns 1,000,000 shares, which is 100 percent. The company raises 1 million dollars at a 4 million dollar pre-money valuation. Post-money is 5 million, so the investor owns 1 million / 5 million = 20 percent. To give them 20 percent, the company issues 250,000 new shares (so 250,000 / 1,250,000 total = 20 percent). The founder still holds 1,000,000 shares but now owns 1,000,000 / 1,250,000 = 80 percent. Her stake fell from 100 to 80 percent, yet 80 percent of a 5 million dollar company (4 million dollars) beats 100 percent of a 4 million dollar company. A later round repeats the pattern on the new, larger share count, so each owner is diluted again. An option pool created before a round dilutes the founders and raises the effective price the investor pays, which is why pool size is often negotiated.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A company worth 9 million dollars pre-money raises 3 million. What is the post-money valuation? 2) In that round, what percentage does the investor own? 3) Define dilution in one sentence. 4) Can dilution leave a founder richer in dollars? 5) What is an option pool? Answers: 1) 9 million + 3 million = 12 million dollars. 2) 3 million / 12 million = 25 percent. 3) the shrinking of each existing owner's percentage when new shares are issued. 4) yes - a smaller percentage of a much larger company can be worth more. 5) a block of shares set aside for future employees.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing pre-money and post-money, which throws off every ownership percentage - always check which one a valuation refers to. Mistake: fearing dilution so much that you under-raise and starve the company, when a smaller slice of a bigger, faster company is often the better outcome. Exit ticket: (a) Post-money valuation equals what? (b) An investor who puts in 2 million dollars at a 10 million dollar post-money valuation owns what percentage? Answers: (a) pre-money valuation plus the amount raised; (b) 2 million / 10 million = 20 percent.

lessons.title: Funding instruments: priced rounds, convertible notes, and SAFEs
lessons.grammar_note: A convertible note is debt that becomes equity; a SAFE is neither debt nor equity until it converts - the words matter.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell apart the three common ways early investments are structured and explain why founders often prefer a SAFE for a first round. Warm-up: why might a tiny startup want to delay setting a firm valuation?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: There are three common instruments. A priced equity round sets a valuation now and sells shares at a fixed price per share; it is precise but slow and costly, since it needs a full legal round and an agreed valuation. A convertible note is a loan that later converts into equity, usually at the next priced round; it charges interest and has a maturity date, so it is technically debt until it converts. A SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) is a simpler promise: the investor gives money now and receives shares later when a priced round happens, with no interest and no maturity date. Both notes and SAFEs let a company raise quickly without fixing a valuation today, which suits very early stages where a fair price is hard to name. They do this with two tools: a valuation cap (a ceiling on the price the early money converts at) and sometimes a discount (a percentage off the next round's price), both of which reward early investors for their greater risk.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example of a cap: an investor puts 100,000 dollars into a SAFE with a 5 million dollar valuation cap. Later the company raises a priced round at a 10 million dollar valuation. The SAFE converts as if the price were only 5 million, so the early investor gets shares at half the price the new investors pay - a reward for the earlier risk. Example of a discount: a 20 percent discount means the SAFE converts at 80 percent of the next round's price per share. Convertible notes add interest - say 5 percent per year - that also converts into shares, and a maturity date by which the note should convert or be repaid, which can create pressure if no round happens. SAFEs drop the interest and maturity, which is why they have become the common first-round instrument for very early startups. A priced round still makes sense once a company is mature enough to name a defensible valuation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which instrument sets a valuation and sells shares today? 2) What makes a convertible note technically debt? 3) What does a valuation cap do for an early investor? 4) If a SAFE has a 20 percent discount, it converts at what fraction of the next round's price? 5) Name one reason founders favor SAFEs for a first raise. Answers: 1) a priced equity round. 2) it is a loan with interest and a maturity date until it converts. 3) it caps the price at which their money converts, giving them more shares if the next valuation is higher. 4) 80 percent. 5) they are fast and simple and avoid setting a valuation too early (also: no interest or maturity date).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: stacking many SAFEs with different caps and forgetting they all convert at the next round, which can dilute founders far more than expected - model the conversion before signing. Mistake: letting a convertible note's maturity date pass without a plan, since it is still a debt that can come due. Exit ticket: (a) What does SAFE stand for? (b) Name the two tools that reward early investors on notes and SAFEs. Answers: (a) Simple Agreement for Future Equity; (b) a valuation cap and a discount.

lessons.title: Term sheets and the key terms that decide control
lessons.grammar_note: 'Economics' and 'control' are the two halves of any term sheet - sort each term into one bucket as you read.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a basic term sheet and explain the common terms that decide control and who gets paid first. Warm-up: is a term sheet a binding contract or a summary of intended terms?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A term sheet is a short, mostly non-binding document that lays out the key terms of a proposed investment before the long legal contracts are drafted. It covers two broad areas: economics (who gets how much money, and when) and control (who gets to decide what). A central economic term is the liquidation preference, which says investors get their money back - often 1 times their investment - before common shareholders see anything when the company is sold. Another is the option pool set aside for future hires. On the control side, a term sheet may define board seats, who sits on the board that governs the company, and protective provisions, a list of decisions (like selling the company or raising more money) that need investor approval. Pro rata rights let an investor buy more shares in future rounds to keep their percentage. Anti-dilution protection adjusts an investor's price if a later round is priced lower. The term sheet is where founders and investors negotiate not just price but power.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example of a liquidation preference: an investor puts in 2 million dollars with a 1 times preference. If the company later sells for 3 million dollars, the investor takes their 2 million first and the remaining 1 million is split among the others. If it sells for 100 million, the preference barely matters, since everyone does well. Example of protective provisions: even an investor who owns only 20 percent may have the right to block a sale of the company, because control terms are separate from ownership percentage. Example of pro rata: an investor who owns 10 percent and has pro rata rights can buy enough of the next round to stay at 10 percent, rather than being diluted. Founders should read a term sheet for more than the valuation: a high valuation paired with a heavy liquidation preference and broad investor vetoes can be worse than a lower valuation on clean, simple terms.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is a term sheet usually binding? 2) What does a 1 times liquidation preference guarantee an investor? 3) What are protective provisions? 4) What do pro rata rights let an investor do? 5) Why can a high valuation with heavy terms be worse than a lower valuation with clean terms? Answers: 1) mostly non-binding - it is a summary of intended terms. 2) they get their investment amount back before common shareholders in a sale. 3) a list of company decisions that require investor approval. 4) buy shares in future rounds to maintain their ownership percentage. 5) harsh control and payout terms can cost founders more in a sale or a vote than a few points of valuation are worth.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: fixating on the headline valuation and ignoring control terms like board seats and vetoes, which decide who really runs the company. Mistake: assuming a term sheet is the final deal, when the binding legal documents come later and can still shift. Exit ticket: (a) Name the term that decides who gets paid first in a sale. (b) What do protective provisions give an investor? Answers: (a) the liquidation preference; (b) the right to approve or block certain major company decisions.

lessons.title: The fundraising process, due diligence, and alternatives
lessons.grammar_note: A signed term sheet is an intention, not a payment - keep the present tense ('we are raising') until the money clears.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the steps of a typical fundraise, explain what investors check during due diligence, and name alternatives to selling equity. Warm-up: after a founder and investor sign a term sheet, is the money in the bank yet?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A fundraise usually runs in steps. Founders prepare a pitch and a data room of documents, build a list of target investors, and take many meetings. An interested investor offers a term sheet. If the founders accept, the investor begins due diligence - a careful check of the company's finances, contracts, technology, team, and legal standing to confirm the story holds up. Only after diligence do lawyers draft and sign the final documents and the money arrives, which can take weeks. Not every company should sell equity, though. Crowdfunding raises small amounts from many people, either as pre-orders of a product (rewards crowdfunding) or as actual shares (equity crowdfunding). Grants are money from governments or foundations that need not be repaid and take no ownership, though they are competitive and restricted in use. Revenue-based financing lends money that is repaid as a fixed percentage of monthly revenue until a set multiple is reached, with no equity given up. Each alternative trades some speed or scale for keeping more ownership and control.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example of due diligence: an investor asks for bank statements, customer contracts, the cap table, employment agreements, and proof the company owns its own technology. A surprise here - an unsigned contract, a messy cap table, a co-founder who never signed over their work - can delay or kill a deal, which is why founders keep clean records from the start. Example of an alternative: a hardware maker runs a rewards crowdfunding campaign, collecting pre-orders that fund the first production run without any investor. Example of revenue-based financing: a company borrows 100,000 dollars and repays 1.5 times that - 150,000 dollars - by handing over 6 percent of monthly revenue until the 150,000 is paid, giving up no shares. A grant might fund early research with no repayment and no dilution at all. The right choice depends on how fast you must grow and how much ownership you are willing to trade.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What happens during due diligence? 2) Put these in order: due diligence, pitch meetings, term sheet, money wired. 3) Which alternative gives money that need not be repaid and takes no ownership? 4) In revenue-based financing, how is the money repaid? 5) Name the two broad types of crowdfunding. Answers: 1) an investor carefully checks the company's finances, contracts, technology, team, and legal standing. 2) pitch meetings, term sheet, due diligence, money wired. 3) a grant. 4) as a fixed percentage of monthly revenue until a set multiple is repaid. 5) rewards crowdfunding (pre-orders) and equity crowdfunding (shares).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a signed term sheet as cash in hand - due diligence and final documents still stand between you and the money, so keep running the company. Mistake: assuming equity is the only option, when grants, crowdfunding, and revenue-based financing may fit a business that does not need venture-scale speed. Exit ticket: (a) What is a data room? (b) Name one way to fund a company without giving up equity. Answers: (a) the organized set of documents investors review during diligence; (b) any one of: a grant, rewards crowdfunding, or revenue-based financing.
